opus-5.5.text:
For me, the central lesson is that taste is not a luxury. It's a form of judgment, and it can be the whole strategy.

When people read about Jobs, they often focus on the personality: the intensity, the "reality distortion field," the way he could be difficult. Those things are real, but I don't think they're the lesson. What struck me most is how much of his work came down to saying no. When he came back to Apple in 1997, the company had a sprawling product line, and he cut it down to almost nothing: a simple grid, consumer and professional, desktop and portable. That wasn't a marketing decision. It was a statement about what the company believed it should be.

The second thing is his insistence that the parts nobody sees still matter. There's the story about his father telling him to finish the back of a cabinet properly, even though it would face the wall. You can treat that as a cute anecdote, but I think it's a philosophy of integrity. If you only care about the surfaces people inspect, you end up with a product, or an organization, that's hollow in the places that eventually matter.

The third lesson is more personal, and it's the one I keep coming back to. He treated his life as finite in a very concrete way. The Stanford speech, asking himself every morning whether he'd want to do what he was about to do if it were his last day: that sounds like a motivational line, but underneath it is a ruthless way of prioritizing. Most of us live as if we have unlimited drafts. He seemed to know he didn't.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: the deepest work comes from caring intensely about a small number of things and refusing to compromise on them, while being willing to let go of almost everything else. The hard part isn't the caring. It's the letting go.

r001.rationale: The response describes caring intensely about a small number of things and letting go of almost everything else as its central lesson, clearly conveying staying focused.

fable-5.1.text:
The central lesson, for me, is that Jobs never confused the product with the company. Most founders think their job is to build an organization, and the product is something the organization produces. Jobs flipped that. He believed the product was the point, and the company was just the machine you build to make the product possible. When he came back to Apple in 1997, the first thing he did wasn't fix the org chart or the finances in the abstract. He cut the product line down to four quadrants and asked, "Which of these would I actually want to use?" Everything else followed from that question.

The second thing I take from him is a kind of ruthless honesty about taste. Jobs had strong opinions about what was good, and he was willing to be wrong loudly rather than be mediocre quietly. A lot of people read the biographies and come away thinking the lesson is "be a jerk to your team," and I think that's the wrong read. The lesson is that someone has to hold the standard, and holding the standard is uncomfortable. Most organizations drift toward consensus, and consensus produces things nobody hates and nobody loves. Jobs refused to let that happen, and he paid a real personal price for it.

And honestly, the third lesson is about patience with the long arc. People remember the iPhone as this sudden stroke of genius, but it was built on NeXT, on Pixar, on a decade of being pushed out and rebuilding himself. The failures weren't detours. They were the training. So when I read about Jobs, I don't come away thinking "be a visionary." I come away thinking: care about the thing itself more than the credit, hold a standard even when it's lonely, and don't mistake a bad decade for the end of the story.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames Jobs’s product-first approach as the central lesson and describes cutting Apple’s product line to focus on what mattered.

astra-6.text: For me, the central lesson is focus. It’s easy to say you want to make something great, but that means deciding what you won’t do—and sticking with those decisions when new opportunities tempt you. What I take from reading about Jobs is the importance of having a clear judgment about what matters, then putting your energy into getting it right.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls focus the central lesson from reading about Jobs and describes sticking to decisions about what matters.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the central lesson is to be clear about what matters and have the courage to focus on it. It’s easy to keep adding things or chasing opportunities. The harder work is deciding what to leave out, then putting real care into what you choose to do.

r001.rationale: Chen Xie names the central lesson as being clear about what matters and having the courage to focus on it.
